Source and attribution

The archive attributes this English wording to F.R.L. (c. 1899); CP 1.135 and files it under Pragmatism. That locator distinguishes the passage from loose internet attributions: readers can return to the named work or section to check translation, surrounding argument, and edition-specific wording.

About Charles Sanders Peirce

Charles Sanders Peirce (1839–1914) was an American logician, scientist, and founder of pragmatism (which he later renamed pragmaticism). Employed irregularly by the Coast Survey and in brief academic posts, he wrote vast unpublished manuscripts.

How to read this passage

Socratic elenchus, scientific method, and pragmatist experimentalism treat inquiry as self-correcting. The ethics of inquiry asks for intellectual honesty. This passage enters that discussion through inquiry, reason, science.

Concepts in this quote

Inquiry
Inquiry is the disciplined pursuit of better questions and answers—philosophy as method rather than dogma.
Reason
Reason is the capacity to give and assess reasons—central to logic, science, ethics, and public argument.
Science
Science appears in this archive as a live philosophical concern—not a slogan. These verified English passages show how thinkers treat science as a problem of judgment, practice, or explanation.
